Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

24.9% of the District of Columbia's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 24.9% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk, including older numbered labels such as A1 to A30 (now shown as AE).

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $384 a year ($32 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $349 and $450. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $349 · Typical $384 · A quarter pay over $450 · A tenth pay $533 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 1,035 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price; a brand-new policy is priced at full risk.

Coverage in force: $464.1 million of building and $136.1 million of contents coverage across all the District of Columbia policies.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood. Past aid paid here is in “Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 501 NFIP flood claims and $5.4 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2011, 2023 and 2020.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2011 ($1,644,463), 2023 ($623,536), 2020 ($572,389). Total paid $5,445,365: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 501 claims since 1978 against 2,187 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 53.7% of claims here paid something. The average paid claim was $20,243.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$20,243
  • Closed with no payment46.3%
  • Claims that paid269

FEMA lists reasons a claim closes without payment, such as damage below the deductible, no flood as the policy defines it, or seepage and drain backup the policy does not cover. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for 65.0% of the 512 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 512 policies reporting one)65.0%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)84.7%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 258 claims paid with a damage figure)1.9%

Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on single-family primary-home policies that report one; many owners insure to the building maximum even when that figure is lower, so the two shares measure different things. The damage share counts every paid claim with a damage figure, all building types.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different prices for the District of Columbia?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $384 a year, but a new one is priced at full risk: about $388 with fees.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Typical cost, single-family homes (median)$384premium plus fees; the middle policy
Typical premium only$264before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Typical cost, policies whose term began in 2025$384515 policies
Typical cost, policies whose term began in 2026$381520 policies
FEMA's full-risk premium (median)$264the price FEMA's model sets; new policies start here
Full-risk premium plus average fees$388close to what a new single-family policy pays
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$414pulled up by a few expensive policies
Average cost, every policy type$854adds condos, rentals and businesses

All from the NFIP policies in force on July 31, 2026. Published figures rarely say which of these they are, or which year; private flood insurance is not in this data. Policies renew on their own anniversaries, so the latest year shows where renewals are heading.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

15.1% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $264, full-risk $264 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$264
  • Median full-risk premium$264
  • Pay below full-risk15.1% of 1,035

Yearly cap: By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Here the median premium is already at or above the median full-risk premium, so the median policy has no gap left to close; any one policy can still sit below its own full-risk price.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Does my town get a community discount?

Not through a community discount: the District of Columbia's only NFIP community has none.

The 0 largest discounts of 0 discounted communities are shown; 1 communities here have no CRS discount.

The Community Rating System cuts NFIP premiums in communities that do extra flood work. A community named for the county covers its unincorporated area only.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 4 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $520,904 for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $488 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Hurricane aid includes wind damage. COVID, fire, ice-storm and tornado aid are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted. FEMA also publishes a separate official policy count, which we have not yet compared for the District of Columbia.

In-force count: 2,187 policy units (from 1,572 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Download check: policies: 1,572 of 1,572 fetched; claims: 501 of 501 fetched.
